query: For high-entropy-alloy materials intended for self-lubricating moving components, what single intervention could reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate across a wide service-temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites prior evidence supporting it, and proposes an experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a tailored nanohierarchical microstructure with spatial composition undulation into high-entropy alloys will form an adaptive friction interface that reduces both the friction coefficient and wear rate across a broad service-temperature range.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventionally processed high-entropy alloy with a relatively homogeneous, coarse-grained microstructure lacking defined nanoscale features.
generation.intervention: Apply a processing route—such as rapid solidification followed by controlled annealing—to induce a nanohierarchical architecture characterized by distributed nanoprecipitates and compositional undulation.
generation.conditions: The alloy is expected to maintain reduced friction and wear performance from room temperature up to around 800 °C under sliding conditions with controlled oxidation levels.
generation.structural_mediator: Ultranano-structured grain boundaries and nanoprecipitates that, under frictional loading, evolve into a self-adaptive, dense nanocrystalline glaze layer which actively buffers shear stresses.
generation.mechanism: The engineered nanostructure enables a staged release of frictional stress at lower temperatures and, at higher temperatures, promotes the formation of a lubricious glaze layer. This multi-type adaptive friction interface minimizes adhesive and oxidative wear, thereby lowering both the coefficient of friction and the wear rate.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to untreated alloys, samples with the nanohierarchical architecture are predicted to exhibit a roughly 30–50% lower friction coefficient and at least a twofold reduction in wear rate under similar sliding conditions.
generation.baseline: The untreated high-entropy alloy typically shows friction coefficients around 0.3 and wear rates on the order of 10⁻⁶ mm³/N·m or higher.
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective under standard sliding conditions and moderate oxidizing environments up to ~800 °C; its benefits may diminish under extreme oxidation or impact conditions beyond the tested range.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of improvement in friction and wear reduction is uncertain without empirical data, and the long-term stability of the adaptive interface under cyclic stresses requires further validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples: one set with conventional processing and one with the tailored processing to induce the nanohierarchical architecture. Conduct sliding wear tests across a temperature range (e.g., room temperature, 400 °C, and 800 °C) under identical tribological conditions while monitoring surface evolution.
measurements: Surface microstructure characterization (e.g., TEM, SEM) pre- and post-testing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nanohierarchically processed samples do not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction (e.g., <30% reduction in friction coefficient and <2× improvement in wear rate) compared to the conventionally processed alloys across the tested temperature range, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

Remarkable Wear Resistance in a Complex Concentrated Alloy with Nanohierarchical Architecture and Composition Undulation

Abstract: AbstractSustained wear damages on the sliding surfaces of alloys are generally the culprit responsible for the failure of various mechanical systems. Inspired by high-entropy effects, here we deliberately deploy nanohierarchical architecture with composition undulation in a Ni50(AlNbTiV)50 complex concentrated alloy, which yields ultralow wear rate within the order of 10−7 to 10−6 mm3/Nm between room temperature and 800 °C. Such remarkable wear resistance heretofore represents one of the highest wear resistance reported for the bulk alloys or composites, and originates from the multi-type adaptive friction interface protection governed by intrinsically nano-coupled grains and nanoprecipitates. This cooperative heterostructure releases gradient frictional stress in stages upon wear at room temperature through the coexistence of multiple deformation pathways while activating a dense nanocrystalline glaze layer upon wear at 800 °C to minimize adhesive and oxidative wear. Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties
